catalog_quote: 2.1.2.1 The Middle Chinese tones The ‘four tones’ (sì shēng 四 聲) of Middle Chinese are píng 平, shǎng 上, qù 去, and rù 入. In our notation they are marked as follows; the English glosses have become conventional translations for the names of the tones: (10) 平 píng < bjaeng ‘level’ no mark 上 shǎng < dzyangX ‘rising’ marked by final -X 去 qù < khjoH ‘departing’ marked by final -H 入 rù < nyip ‘entering’ marked by final -p, -t, or -k The names of the tones were evidently chosen to be both descriptive of the tones they denote and examples of them; thus 平 píng < bjaeng itself is a píngshēng word, 上 shàng ~ shǎng < dzyangX is a shǎngshēng word, and so forth. ... The rùshēng category includes all and only those words that ended in -p, -t, or -k; these codas have been lost in Mandarin but are preserved in some southern dialects, such as Cantonese. audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation from Baxter & Sagart 2014 sec. 2.1.2.1 is verbatim on printed p.14 (PDF p.29) of the held publisher PDF and on the held page image; the domain quote (pp.9-10) is verbatim in the held text excerpt. (2) Deciding source: a 2014 OUP historical-reconstruction monograph by the field's leading reconstructors; its MC chapter is a standard, current statement of the Qieyun system. Middle Chinese is a philologically attested stage whose entire phonological record is organised by the four tone categories; no description of MC word stress exists or can exist, and the record already says so. (3) Better-targeted MC works exist (Pulleyblank 1984 monograph; Mei 1970 on tone phonetics) but are paywalled and would only add phonetic detail to tone_note, not alter the TONAL coding; Glottolog's listed grammars (Zograf, Halliday, Pulleyblank 1970-71) are text grammars/re

Would refine tone_note ('phonetic pitch values not recoverable', currently via Wikipedia<Norman) with a primary; silent on word stress.
